items.name: The sea in late October and November
items.teaser: About 18–19C on average in November, falling through the month; early November often reads 18–21C
items.story: The honest figure for Split's sea in November is 18 to 19C, and the sources differ because they use different data. Weather2Travel and Beach-weather both give 18C and call it too cold for long swims. Seatemperature.net gives a 19C average with a 16 to 22C range, and its daily tables for recent years show mostly 18 to 21C in early November. The water loses heat week by week, so the last days of October are the better end. A hard bura can drop it, and chill the air, in a day.
items.why: Swim at midday on a calm, sunny day, and keep a wetsuit aboard for anyone who feels the cold.
facts: Late Oct to end Nov, cooling week by week
Bačvice, Kašjuni and the rocks below Marjan, or the islands

items.story: Jadrolinija's 2026 timetable for line 631, Split to Supetar on Brač, has high season from 1 June to 30 September and low season from 1 October to 31 December. The crossing takes about 50 minutes, with departures from Split from about 05:00 to just before midnight, some not running on Sundays and holidays. One version of the timetable says the line did not sail on Sundays in October. Travel guides say the Jadrolinija summer catamaran to Hvar Town runs only in summer, while a year-round catamaran goes to Jelsa via Bol. For Vis, guides name the car ferry and a Kapetan Luka catamaran.
items.why: Book the car ferry ahead on Friday evenings and holiday eves; low season means fewer boats, not empty ones.

items.name: The olive harvest and the new oil, Brač and Šolta
items.teaser: Picking runs from October into November; Brač and Šolta both carry EU protected oils
items.story: The olives come in from October, and in many years into November, when families go back to the islands to pick. Brač oil has EU protected designation of origin since January 2022, made from at least 80 per cent Oblica, and the island calls itself Croatia's largest olive-growing area; the Supetar agricultural cooperative led the application. Šolta's oil was protected in October 2016, and in 2026 the Zlatna Šoltanka association, about 20 producers, won two golds at the NYIOOC in New York. New oil is green, bitter and peppery.
items.why: Taste the new oil on bread with nothing else, and buy it from the producer on the island.
facts: Oct–Nov; first new oil from late October, by weather

items.name: Martinje, Wednesday 11 November
items.teaser: St Martin's Day, when the must becomes wine and is 'baptised'; no Split event was found
items.story: St Martin's Day falls on 11 November, and across Croatia it is the day the young wine is baptised: the must has finished fermenting and is wine. The tradition is strongest in the north, in Istria, the Zagreb hills and Slavonia, where whole villages hold feasts with a mock priest, goose and chestnuts. Around Split it is quieter, but wine bars and konobas open the year's first bottles. No 2026 Martinje event in Split or on the islands was found when this was checked, so treat it as a reason to order, not a festival.
items.why: Ask for this year's wine by name on the 11th, and have it with roast meat or chestnuts.

items.name: Fritule, from the end of November
items.teaser: Small round Dalmatian doughnuts with raisins, rum and lemon zest, sold at the Advent stalls on the Riva
items.story: Fritule are the Advent sweet of Dalmatia: a soft yeast dough with raisins, rum or rakija and lemon or orange zest, dropped by the spoon into hot oil and dusted with icing sugar. Homes make them for Christmas Eve. In Split they come with the Advent stalls on the Riva, from the end of November or early December, and a 2022 report described three of the Riva stalls as sweet stalls selling fritule and pancakes. They are eaten hot, standing, from a paper cone. No 2026 price was found.
items.why: Buy them from a stall frying to order, not from a tray that has gone cold.
facts: With Advent, expected from about 28 Nov 2026 to early Jan

items.name: Clocks back, then two holidays
items.teaser: Clocks go back on Sun 25 Oct; All Saints on Sun 1 Nov and Remembrance Day on Wed 18 Nov are public holidays
items.story: Croatia follows the European clock change: at 03:00 on Sunday 25 October 2026 the clocks go back one hour, and by mid-November the sun sets in Split at about 16:15. All Saints' Day, Sunday 1 November, is a public holiday; families visit the graves, and the cemeteries fill with candles and chrysanthemums. Wednesday 18 November, Remembrance Day for the victims of the Homeland War and of Vukovar, has been a public holiday since 2020. On holidays shops close or shorten their hours and ferries can run a Sunday timetable.
items.why: Provision the day before each holiday, and plan sunset drinks for about 16:00 from November.

items.name: Za Križen, Hvar: the night of Maundy Thursday
items.teaser: Six villages, six barefoot cross-bearers, about 25 km through the night; UNESCO-listed in 2009
items.story: On the night from Maundy Thursday to Good Friday, six processions leave Jelsa, Pitve, Vrisnik, Svirče, Vrbanj and Vrboska at the same time and walk through all six villages, about 25 km in eight hours, without meeting. Each is led by a cross-bearer who walks barefoot or in socks; people put their names down for the role up to twenty years ahead. The kantaduri sing the Lamentations of the Virgin, a 15th-century text. The first written record is from 1658. UNESCO inscribed it in 2009. In 2027 Easter is on 28 March.
items.why: Watch from one village square, in silence; it is a devotion, not a show.
facts: Night of Thu 25 to Fri 26 March 2027

items.name: Sudamja, St Domnius' Day, 7 May
items.teaser: Split's own feast: Mass and procession on the Riva, the Sudamja fair, ten days of events around it
items.story: St Domnius, Sveti Duje, was bishop of Salona and was martyred around 304 in Diocletian's persecution; his cathedral is now the emperor's mausoleum. Split keeps his feast and City Day on 7 May. In 2026 the programme ran from 30 April to 10 May with more than 170 events: the solemn Mass and procession on the Riva on the 7th, the Sudamja fair of local producers and craftspeople on Voćni trg from 6 to 8 May, concerts on the Riva and Taste of Split at the Prokurative. In 2027 the 7th is a Friday.
items.why: Be on the Riva for the morning procession, then walk the fair on Voćni trg.

bougie.title: 2001 — Zinfandel's lost parent found in Kaštela
bougie.desc: How a Californian grape was traced to a few old vines in a mixed plot between Split and Trogir, and what it is called now.
bougie.lede: California's Zinfandel had no known home. In 2001 a DNA test matched it to a handful of old vines called Crljenak Kaštelanski in Ivica Radunić's mixed vineyard at Kaštel Novi, fifteen minutes from Split. Ten years later a dried leaf in a Split herbarium gave the grape its older Dalmatian name: Tribidrag.
paras: The hunt was led by Carole Meredith, a grape geneticist at UC Davis, with Ivan Pejić and Edi Maletić of the Zagreb Faculty of Agriculture. Plavac Mali was the first suspect, but it was not Zinfandel. Meredith sought help from American producers, among them Miljenko (Mike) Grgić, the Napa winemaker born in Croatia. The Zagreb team then searched old Dalmatian vineyards for forgotten varieties, collecting leaves for DNA.

In Kaštel Novi they found a mixed plot about 35 years old belonging to Ivica Radunić. Samples of a vine he called Crljenak Kaštelanski matched Zinfandel. The dates differ: Grgich Hills says Maletić found the vine on 7 September 2000; Radunić recalls hearing from Meredith in September 2001; the SOMM Journal gives the result as 18 December 2001. The number of vines is argued too, from nine to eleven in the plot, with more later found near Omiš.

A 2011 paper reported that a herbarium leaf about 90 years old, labelled Tribidrag and kept in Split's Natural History Museum, had the same DNA, and suggested the grape was grown in Croatia from the early 15th century; one source cites a 1488 barrel shipped from Venice to Apulia. The Zagreb team's 2004 paper had already shown Plavac Mali to be its offspring with Dobričić. Pejić still says there is no proof the variety was born in Croatia. Plantings are now about 250 ha across Dalmatia.

_corrections: Old [history] card: Plavac Mali was not 'identified in 2001 by UC Davis DNA analysis as the Dalmatian ancestor of California Zinfandel'. Plavac Mali is the offspring of Zinfandel/Tribidrag and Dobričić (Maletić, Pejić et al., AJEV 2004); the 2001 match was with Crljenak Kaštelanski.

Old [drink] text: 'Plavac Mali ... ancestor of Zinfandel and Primitivo' is wrong for the same reason; Zinfandel, Primitivo, Crljenak Kaštelanski and Tribidrag are one variety, and Plavac Mali its child.
The discovery date is disputed: 7 Sep 2000 (Grgich Hills), Sep 2001 (Radunić's recollection), 18 Dec 2001 (SOMM Journal); some retailers say 2002.
The number of old vines in Radunić's plot is disputed: nine (one source), the sampled vine plus eight more (SOMM Journal), or eleven (Taste of Adriatic); 'nine' is kept only as one reading.
Tribidrag identification: the herbarium paper is 2011 (PubMed), while Jancis Robinson places the analysis in 2008; the earliest written record is given variously as the 15th century, 1488 and 1518.
